title: Cardiovascular risk and subclinical hypothyroidism: focus on lipids and new emerging risk factors. What is the evidence?
source_type: Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association
text_summary: 本文综述亚临床甲状腺功能减退与心血管风险的证据。亚临床甲减以TSH升高而游离甲状腺激素正常为特征，尤其当TSH超过10 mU/L时，常伴总胆固醇和LDL胆固醇升高以及不利的胆固醇比值；风险随TSH升高和向显性甲减进展而增加。除血脂异常外，胰岛素抵抗、内皮功能障碍、动脉僵硬、C反应蛋白、同型半胱氨酸和凝血变化等因素也可能共同促进动脉粥样硬化。左甲状腺素改善血脂和心血管指标的研究结果并不完全一致，因此应先确认持续性TSH升高，再结合TSH水平、症状、年龄及其他心血管危险因素个体化决定治疗。
text:
Reviews
Cardiovascular Risk and Subclinical Hypothyroidism:
Focus on Lipids and New Emerging Risk Factors.
What Is the Evidence?
Leonidas H. Duntas 1 and Leonard Wartofsky 2,3
Controversy remains as to the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) associated with subclinical hypothyroidism
(SCH), deﬁned as an increased serum thyrotropin (TSH) concentration with normal free thyroxine and tri-
iodothyronine levels. Substantial evidence indicates altered cholesterol and lipoprotein metabolism in SCH when
serum TSH is above 10 mU =L. Observed abnormalities include elevated plasma levels of total cholesterol (TC)
and low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C); the altered TC =high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C)
and LDL-C=HDL-C ratios suggest a potential accelerated risk for CVD. The inﬂuence of SCH on lipids is directly
proportional to the degree of TSH elevation and becomes more signiﬁcant with the progression from SCH to
overt disease, thereby accelerating any propensity to atherosclerosis. Although many clinicians may tend to
ignore SCH with TSH levels <10, it is apparent that an enhanced CV risk could apply to these individuals,
perhaps compounded by insulin resistance and ampliﬁed by the copresence of other risk factors such as endo-
thelial dysfunction and elevated C-reactive protein.
Introduction
T
he onset of hypothyroidism is a progressive process
associated with impairment of function of multiple or-
gan systems. In regard to the cardiovascular (CV) system,
cardiac dysfunction and heart damage may be induced via
an increment of highly atherogenic low-density lipoprotein-
cholesterol (LDL-C) particles, induction of diastolic hyperten-
sion, stiffening of central arteries with endothelial dysfunction,
and altered coagulation parameters (1–3).
Subclinical hypothyroidism (SCH), which is deﬁned as
elevation of serum thyrotropin (TSH) with normal free thy-
roxine (FT4) and free triiodothyronine (FT3) concentrations,
is more common in women, especially at older ages, with a
prevalence ranging from 10% to 15% (4–7). In most, but not
all, circumstances, SCH may be considered equivalent to an
early or mildly hypothyroid state. A precise upper limit TSH
cutoff level is debatable, but >95% of normal individuals will
have a TSH <2.5 mU=L (7), so values greater than 2.5 mU =L
can be considered suspicious for early or mild thyroid dys-
function (8).
In several studies, SCH has been associated with markers
of CV risk and cardiac impairment, as even minor deviations
from the serum TSH norm may accelerate the development
of atherosclerosis and produce changes in CV performance
(9,10). Nevertheless, the evidence is controversial, since few
inconsistent data exist regarding the effects of levothyroxine
(LT4) treatment of SCH on both symptoms and various
biochemical parameters related to CV risk (11,12).
Recently, abnormalities in several parameters considered
risk factors for CV disease (CVD) have been identiﬁed in
patients with SCH. These risk factors include serum homo-
cysteine (Hct) and C-reactive protein (CRP), endothelial
dysfunction, and arterial stiffness (13). The prevalence of
antithyroperoxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies sug-
gestive of underlying Hashimoto’s disease directly paral-
lels the prevalence of TSH elevations in SCH. Consequently,
Hashimoto’s disease is considered to be the most likely cause
of SCH. With progressive thyroid failure with time, SCH
gradually evolves into overt hypothyroidism, thereby ren-
dering patients liable to an increased CV risk with the ath-
erogenic process having been initiated long before the clinical

diagnosis of hypothyroidism is established. This thesis is
indirectly supported by the observation that patients with
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis aged over 50 years exhibit a threefold
increase in CV hospital admissions, indicating increased
morbidity compared to controls (14).
The aim of this article is to review the existing evidence
that SCH represents a risk for CVD, with special focus on
evaluating whether other recently identiﬁed risk factors may
be contributing to the underlying pathogenesis by com-
pounding the effect of lipid alterations in SCH. Although a
number of review articles and meta-analyses have addressed
the issue of hyperlipidemia in SCH during the last decade,
our analysis will reassess the data with a focus on evolving
information on newly described risk factors and the role that
they may play in atherogenesis.
SCH and Lipids
Historic background and pathophysiology
An association between hypothyroidism and hypercho-
lesterolemia has been appreciated since the 1930s when ani-
mal studies demonstrated that hypothyroidism induced by
high cholesterol feeding could be prevented by supplemen-
tation with thyroid preparations (15). These ﬁndings were
conﬁrmed in the 1960s when rabbits fed on a high cholesterol
diet became hypothyroid to the same extent as the post-
thyroidectomy group (16). During the same decade, case-
control studies comparing autopsy ﬁndings in patients with
myxedema and in controls revealed a higher prevalence of
coronary arteriosclerosis in those with myxedema and hy-
pertension (17,18). The elucidation of the molecular nature of
the LDL receptor in the 1980s and the discovery that its ac-
tivity is regulated by thyroid hormone further conﬁrmed the
relationship between thyroid hormone and lipids (19,20).
Given the demonstrated link between lipids and CVD, an
indirect role of thyroid functional state and propensity for
CVD has been questioned. Subsequent studies have clariﬁed
the mechanism of action of thyroid hormone on lipid syn-
thesis and the consequences of thyroid failure on lipid metab-
olism, and have been recently reviewed (3,21). Plasma lipid
levels are dependent on metabolism of very-low-density
lipoprotein apolipoprotein (apo) B, which is the precursor of
intermediate-density lipoprotein and LDL-C. It is also rele-
vant that the concentration of cholesteryl ester transfer pro-
tein, a key enzyme for reverse cholesterol transport, is highly
sensitive to thyroid hormone alterations (22).
In an earlier study, the metabolic spectrum of progressive
thyroid failure was investigated in 86 women at various stages
of hypothyroidism and compared with controls (23). LDL-C
was statistically signiﬁcantly elevated in grade III hypothy-
roidism (TSH >12 mU=L), while total cholesterol (TC),
triglyceride, and apo B were clearly increased only in overt
hypothyroidism (with diminished T4). That high LDL-C in
SCH contributes to the pathophysiological explanation of
the association of coronary heart disease (CHD) with SCH is
consistent with the association of elevated TC =high-density
lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-C) ratio and development of ath-
erosclerosis. It is noteworthy that in the transition from hypo-
thyroidism to euthyroidism, changes in LDL-C and HDL-C
correlate with the improvement in FT4 levels and not with the
polymorphisms in the LDL receptor or the cholesterol ester
transfer protein gene (24).
Recent studies have shown an association between circu-
lating levels of oxidized-LDL (oxi-LDL) and angiographically
documented CVD (25). Accordingly, oxi-LDL may substan-
tially contribute to CVD in patients with increased produc-
tion of oxi-LDL as they have been associated with CVD
independently of all other clinical and lipid parameters, with
the exception of Lp(a). Increased oxi-LDL levels, expressed as
oxidized phospholipid content per particle of apo B-100, have
been reported in patients with SCH as compared to controls,
and the levels were higher in overt hypothyroidism (26).
Levels were strongly inﬂuenced by smoking, and a deleteri-
ous inﬂuence of smoking has been demonstrated on the lipid
proﬁle in both overt and subclinical hypothyroid patients
(27). Women smokers with SCH had higher TSH and ex-
hibited increased TC and LDL-C by 16% and 28%, respec-
tively. Also noteworthy was the ﬁnding that postprandial
lipemia, which plays an essential role in the pathogenesis of
atherosclerosis, was found increased as compared to controls
in overt hypothyroid patients and in those with a TSH level of
5.5 mU=L or greater (28).
Moreover, a recent study from Japan, evaluating 26 pa-
tients with SCH (mean baseline TSH of 9.4 mU =L), found
increased levels of non-HDL-C, deﬁned as the difference
between the TC and HDL-C. Non-HDL-C can be considered
a better marker of CVD than LDL-C because it contains
all cholesterol of the lipoproteins (29). A reduction in non-
HDL-C levels seen following LT4 treatment was assumed
to be a result of the induced decrease of serum LDL-C con-
centrations.
Epidemiologic evidence and evaluation
Epidemiologic data on an inﬂuence of SCH on lipids are
somewhat conﬂicting (30). There is conclusive evidence sup-
porting a weak association between SCH and serum lipids
starting at a level of TSH <5m U=L and assuming signiﬁ-
cance on approaching a TSH level of approximately 10 mU =L
and above, thereby contributing to an increased CV risk in
SCH. In the initial large Whickham cohort study, no associ-
ation between SCH and CHD was detected (31). In the 20-
year follow-up study of this cohort, a higher incidence of
progression to overt hypothyroidism was observed, starting
at an original TSH value of approximately 2.5 mU =L, but no
association between raised TSH levels, antithyroid anti-
bodies, and the development of CVD was found (4).
In the Colorado thyroid disease prevalence study of 25,862
subjects, 9.5% had SCH (deﬁned as a TSH >5.1 mU=L) (32).
In this survey, serum TC averaged 214, 224, and 251 mg =dL
in euthyroid, SCH, and hypothyroid patients, respectively,
with these differences being statistically signiﬁcant ( p <
0.001).
In another study investigating the prevalence of SCH at
different levels of TC in 1191 middle-aged men and women,
an overall prevalence of 7.6% in women and of 1.9% in men
was observed (33). The lowest prevalence of SCH of 4% was
seen in the <5 mmol=L( <193.7 mg=dL) cholesterol group,
and the prevalence increased to 10.3% in the highest choles-
terol group. A signiﬁcant increase of 0.09 mmol =L (3.5 mg =
dL) in TC has been estimated in men and of 0.16 mmol =L
(6.2 mg=dL) in women for every 1 mU =L elevation in serum
TSH (34). Thus, an increase of TSH of approximately 5 mU =L
in women, assuming a TSH value of 3 mU =L above the norm,

is accompanied by an increase of 0.27 mmol =L (10.5 mg =dL)
in TC, with an attendant potential increase in CV risk.
In a cross-sectional study of 2799 white and black par-
ticipants, aged 70–79 years, a positive association between
TSH and TC was found in both racial groups, although older
blacks had a lower prevalence of thyroid dysfunction com-
pared with older white adults (35). A TSH level >5.5 mU=L
was associated with a 0.23 mmol =L( 9 m g =dL) higher TC
level.
In a large cross-sectional study in Korea including 66,260
subjects between 20 and 80 years of age, the prevalence
of SCH was, in accordance with expectations, higher in
women, although somewhat lower than in other countries,
and the women exhibited statistically signiﬁcant elevated
TC and LDL-C levels (36). On the other hand, an analysis
from the U.S. National Health and Nutritional Examina-
tion Survey (NHANES) III including 215 participants with
a TSH value of 6.7–14.9 mU =L showed no relation be-
tween SCH and TC, LDL-C, or triglyceride when adjusted
for confounding variables such as age, sex, or the use of
drugs (37).
In a health survey in Busselton, Western Australia, TC,
triglyceride, HDL-C, LDL-C, TSH, and FT4 values were
measured in 631 subjects and compared with those of 1477
euthyroid participants (38). TC and LDL-C were found
higher in subjects with SCH than in controls. Values of
LDL-C were signiﬁcantly increased after adjustment for age
and sex in both the cross-sectional analysis and the longitu-
dinal components of the investigation, representing strong
evidence for SCH as an independent risk factor for CVD.
However, the association was statistically signiﬁcant only for
those with a serum TSH >10 mU=L (39).
The relationship between serum lipids and TSH was
evaluated in the most recent, ﬁfth Tromso study, a cross-
sectional epidemiological survey and nested case-control
study that included 5143 individuals (40). TC and LDL-C
were signiﬁcantly higher and apo A1 levels signiﬁcantly
lower in 84 SCH patients compared with 145 controls. Al-
though there was a positive association between serum TSH
and TC and LDL-C values, it did not achieve statistical sig-
niﬁcance in the women after adjustment for age and body
mass index (BMI).
Further, the HUNT study, a cross-sectional, population-
based study including 30,656 individuals without known
thyroid disease, demonstrated that increasing levels of TSH
across the entire reference range were linearly associated
with deranged lipid concentrations (41). These important
ﬁndings point out that SCH indicated by TSH levels within
the ostensibly clinically ‘‘normal’’ reference range may have
long-term repercussions on CV health via an association
with serum lipids. Based on the data available, however, the
association between SCH and CVD may not be entirely ex-
plained by dyslipidemia alone.
Translation of these epidemiologic lipid data into a clinical
outcome was provided by a retrospective analysis from
Rotterdam (42). This cross-sectional analysis of 1149 women
aged 55 years or over demonstrated that SCH was inde-
pendently associated with both atherosclerosis and myocar-
dial infarction after adjustment for several CV risk factors.
However, these results are in contrast with the earlier Car-
diovascular Health Study, in which analysis of 3678 men and
women did not reveal any difference in the prevalence of
angina, myocardial infarction, and stroke between SCH and
euthyroid individuals (43). SCH has been reported as an
independent risk factor for myocardial infarction in elderly
women, while high serum TSH has recently been associated
with multivessel disease, although it does not represent
a determinant of coronary artery disease in patients with
serum TSH within the normal levels (44).
SCH and Metabolic Syndrome
It is generally well accepted that hypothyroidism and the
metabolic syndrome both are associated with increased risk
for CVD. Studies have examined a possible relationship be-
tween hypothyroidism and the metabolic syndrome by
variously correlating metabolic parameters with either thy-
roid hormone concentrations (e.g., FT4 and FT3) or TSH. In a
cross-sectional cohort study including 2703 participants and
investigating the hypothesis that thyroid function is associ-
ated with components of the metabolic syndrome, a recip-
rocal relationship was observed between FT4 and FT3 and
TC and LDL-C within the euthyroid range (45). TSH was
signiﬁcantly associated with the homeostasis model assess-
ment index for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) after adjust-
ment for age and sex. A cardinal ﬁnding of this study was a
signiﬁcant association between low normal FT4 and insulin
resistance that related to four out of ﬁve metabolic syndrome
traits, thereby implicating low normal FT4 as an indicator
of increased CV risk. Moreover, even in euthyroidism the
lipid levels were associated with thyroid function, indicat-
ing increased CV risk in patients with low normal thyroid
function (45). Recently, it has been demonstrated that insu-
lin resistance may modify the relationship between lipids
and thyroid function and that the association of TSH with
LDL-C varies depending on the absence or presence of in-
sulin sensitivity, since it is shown to be strongly positive in
insulin-resistant subjects (46). The association between FT4
concentrations within the normal reference range and lip-
ids in euthyroid subjects was even stronger than that be-
tween TSH levels and lipids. However, in a cross-sectional,
community-based study including 117 women, a strong pos-
itive association between TSH and lipid parameters with
higher CV risk was observed solely at low insulin sensitivity
(47). The interaction was even stronger for lipid risk factors
associated with insulin resistance, while the interaction be-
tween thyroid function and insulin sensitivity has been sug-
gested as constituting an important component of diabetic
dyslipidemia.
In 87 euthyroid obese patients with BMI >40 kg=m
2, se-
rum TSH levels were found higher than in women with BMI
<40 kg=m2 and were positively correlated with BMI, leptin,
leptin=BMI ratio, body surface area, and insulin sensitivity
(HOMA) (48). It was therefore suggested that TSH may rep-
resent a marker of energy balance in markedly obese eu-
thyroid patients. Based on these data, it would appear likely
that insulin resistance underlies the role of mild thyroid de-
ﬁciency, dyslipidemia, and altered endothelial dysfunction
in the progression of CVD (49). Moreover, in middle-aged
women, SCH is usually associated with hypertension and
elevated TC =HDL-C ratio, and often with hypertriglycer-
idemia, which are all confounders of metabolic syndrome
and liable to increase the risk of atherosclerosis in these
women (50).

Systematic Review of LT4 Treatment
Effects on Lipids
Given a number of reasons other than hypothyroidism for
modest elevations of serum TSH, there is general consensus
that T4 therapy should not be initiated unless the labora-
tory abnormality is conﬁrmed. Once the diagnosis of SCH is
secured by repeated TSH measurements 2 months apart,
treatment decision should be made on an individual basis as
has recently been suggested (51,52). The goal of LT4 re-
placement in SCH is to restore euthyroidism (serum TSH
0.5–2 mU=L) and reduce the impact of serum lipids and other
factors associated with increased risk of CVD. In a meta-
analysis of 13 trials evaluating the effect of LT4 treatment on
lipids in SCH, the most signiﬁcant results were seen in those
subjects with higher initial TSH levels and =or serum TC
>240 mg=dL (53).
Over the past few years, numerous reports of studies have
described a spectrum of effects of SCH on various risk factors
for CVD. The multiplicity of published data has included
both observational studies and large clinical trials. However,
the impact of many of the observational studies is limited by
small population size, short follow-up, variable deﬁnitions
of SCH, and the absence of randomization or appropriate
controls. To gain insight into the potential role in SCH of
alterations in risk factors for CVD in addition to lipids, we
performed a systematic review of the literature published
since the latter meta-analysis on the efﬁcacy of LT4 treatment
in reduction of lipid (see Table 1). We evaluated all articles
included in MEDLINE, accessed through PubMed on the
basis of Medical Subject Heading terms. Evidence for efﬁcacy
was graded according to a grading scheme recommended by
the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development
and Evaluation Working Group (54). Strength of evidence
was classiﬁed into four categories comprising I (strong), II
(moderate, further research is likely to affect the conﬁdence
in the estimates), III (low, further research is very likely to
greatly affect conﬁdence in the estimates), and IV (very low,
any estimate is very uncertain).
The ﬁrst double-blind study after the meta-analysis of
Danese et al . (53) showing that LT4 replacement therapy in
SCH has a signiﬁcant beneﬁcial effect on both LDL-C and
clinical symptoms was the Basel Thyroid Study (55). Among
the 66 enrolled women with SCH, the decrease of the LDL-C
after 50 weeks of treatment with LT4 was more pronounced
in those patients with a TSH >12 mU=L or increased LDL-C
at baseline. Similar results were seen in two other random-
ized, placebo-controlled studies that reported signiﬁcantly
reduced TC and LDL-C in 45 and 40 patients, respectively,
after LT4 treatment over 24 weeks (56,57). In contrast, a
randomized study with 40 patients ( n ¼ 23 on LT4) did not
ﬁnd any effect of LT4 after 6 months of treatment (58). Sim-
ilarly, a cross-sectional study including 37 patients did not
observe any LT4 effect on lipids except in those with base-
line TC >240 mg=dL (59). On the other hand, the above-
mentioned ﬁfth Tromso study, an intervention trial with
LT4-treated patients with SCH, resulted in signiﬁcant re-
duction of apo B, LDL-C, and TC only in those whose TSH
was reduced to the range 0.2–2 mU =L (40) (Table 1).
Finally, a very recent randomized, double-blind study as-
sessed CV risk factors and quality of life in 100 SCH patients
(mean TSH: 6.1 mU =L) treated with 100 mg of LT4 or placebo

for 12 weeks. LT4 treatment was associated with signiﬁcant
reductions of TC, LDL-C, and waist =hip ratio as well as im-
provement in ﬂow-mediated vascular dilatation (60). In ad-
dition, the study indicated that increases in FT4 levels were
the best predictor of TC reduction and the strongest correlate
to reduced CV risk in SCH.
Newly Identiﬁed Risk Factors
Homocysteine
There is strong evidence suggesting that hyperhomocys-
teinemia constitutes an independent risk factor for the pro-
gression of atherosclerosis (61). Hct has been shown to be
increased in overt hypothyroidism and decreased in hyper-
thyroidism, suggesting that thyroid hormone is an essen-
tial regulator of either production or turnover of serum Hct
(62–64). The relation between hypothyroidism and Hct and
LDL-C was evaluated in 32 participants of the U.S. NHANES
III with TSH >20 mU=L (65). A statistically signiﬁcant rela-
tionship was observed between TSH and TC and LDL-C with
odds ratios (95% conﬁdence interval) of 4.9 and 8.0, respec-
tively. The pathogenesis of increased Hct in hypothyroid-
ism may be linked to the reduced glomerular ﬁltration rate
and clearance, and partly explained by changes in folate me-
tabolism induced by alterations of degradative enzyme activ-
ity (66).
In another cross-sectional, double-blind, placebo-
controlled trial, serum Hct levels were statistically signiﬁ-
cantly increased in 61 overtly hypothyroid patients, but not
in 63 subjects with SCH, as compared to 40 euthyroid con-
trols (67). Several other studies assessing the Hct concentra-
tions in SCH failed to show any association of SCH with
serum Hct levels. For example, in a prospective study in
Austria, fasting total plasma Hct levels measured in SCH
were not increased and remained unaltered after LT4 treat-
ment (68). Another prospective investigation of 47 patients
with SCH did not indicate any signiﬁcant change in Hct
levels as compared with controls with no association between
SCH and hyperhomocysteinemia detected (69). In another
trial, levels of Hct were measured both during fasting and
after methionine intake in 12 patients with SCH before and
after 6 months LT4 administration, and no signiﬁcant chan-
ges could be detected in comparison to baseline values (70).
In a small group of adolescent patients with SCH, the Hct
levels were also not signiﬁcantly different than controls (71).
Further, in the cross-sectional New Mexico Elder Health
Survey, no difference could be detected between Hct levels in
overt hypothyroidism and SCH versus controls (72). In the
same survey, only those participants with a TSH >10 mU=L
had a signiﬁcantly higher prevalence of CVD, and Hct values
correlated with serum FT4 levels, indicating that FT4 is an
independent determinant of Hct concentrations as has re-
cently been reported (73). In sum, the overall evidence from
these studies does not suggest an effect of SCH (at least with
TSH levels <10 mU=L), and it is therefore unlikely that Hct
levels contribute to increased CV risk in SCH.
C-reactive protein
Increased levels of high-sensitive C-reactive protein
(hsCRP) have consistently been associated with CVD and
represent a sensitive prognostic tool in determining CV risk
(74,75). The half-life of CRP is about 19 hours in both health
and disease, thus representing a stable marker of the inﬂam-
matory process (76). Measured by a high-sensitive immuno-
assay, hsCRP has been demonstrated to be additive to LDL-C
and TC=LDL-C ratio in predicting CV events (77). Circulating
CRP levels that are slightly increased, but within the healthy
normal reference range, have been linked to metabolic syn-
drome, suggesting a pre- or proinﬂammatory state, a condi-
tion often detected in middle-aged women (78,79).
The prospective study by Christ-Crain et al . (67) was the
ﬁrst to show that CRP levels increase with progressive thy-
roid failure and may represent an additional CV risk factor
in hypothyroidism. CRP levels were signiﬁcantly increased
in both overt hypothyroidism and SCH as compared to con-
trols, though no correlation with thyroid hormone levels was
found. However, in a study evaluating the relationship be-
tween hsCRP and FT4 levels in a large population of euthy-
roid hyperlipidemic patients, it was shown that hsCRP was
negatively associated with FT4 levels in nonsmoking hyper-
lipidemic patients, indicating that low FT4 may constitute
a new biomarker of CV risk (79). Recently, it has been re-
ported that 84 patients with SCH had signiﬁcantly increased
serum hsCRP levels as compared with controls and that the
values were reduced after treatment with LT4 (80), but this
was not seen in the series of patients reported by Perez et al .
(81). Further, in a study of 353 patients with various thyroid
diseases designed to evaluate whether CRP levels could dif-
ferentiate between inﬂammatory and noninﬂammatory thy-
roid conditions, it was shown that CRP plays only a marginal
role in the diagnosis of thyroid disease other than in the
case of subacute thyroiditis (82). However, all these data do
not respond to the question whether autoimmune thyroid
disease, the most frequent cause of SCH, plays a role in
the elevation of CRP, which could partly explain the Hak
data (42).
Coagulation parameters, central arterial stiffness,
and intima-medial thickness
Several studies have reported alterations of the coagula-
tion system in overt and SCH that seems to be dependent on
the degree of severity of the thyroid disorder (83–85). Pa-
tients with overt hypothyroidism have an increased risk of
bleeding due to a hypocoagulable state (86). Recently, it has
been shown that patients with SCH or moderate thyroid
failure have decreased ﬁbrinolytic activity presenting as low
d-dimers and high levels of tissue plasminogen activator and
plasminogen activator inhibitor type 1 (PAI-1), and serum
levels of FT4 directly correlated with ﬁbrinogen levels (87).
These alterations result in decreased ﬁbrinolytic activity and
increased risk for myocardial infarction, particularly due to
the high PAI-1 levels in mild thyroid failure. Women with
SCH (TSH >6m U=L) had signiﬁcantly higher activity of
Factor VII than euthyroid controls, implying a propensity to
a hypercoagulable state (88). These changes in coagulation
factors have not been seen universally in SCH, with no dif-
ferences detected in parameters of ﬁbrinolysis between SCH
and controls in one study although Factor VII activity was
seen to correlate inversely with HDL-C levels (89).
Both enhanced central aortic pressure and central arterial
stiffness have been reported in patients with SCH, therefore
representing independent risk factors for CVD (90). Ac-

cordingly, a study assessing the cardiac and arterial function
in SCH described increased arterial stiffness in 19 patients
with mean serum TSH of 8.8 mU =L (91). After 6 months of
LT4 therapy, parameters indicating arterial stiffness fell to
control levels. Arterial stiffening has been indicated by
changes in the velocity of the brachial-ankle pulse wave, and
changes in the latter correlate with the presence of ische-
mic heart disease. Improvement in the brachial-ankle pulse
wave velocity is seen after LT4 therapy (92). It has also
been described that endothelial function, which has a piv-
otal role in the maintenance of vascular integrity, is im-
paired in SCH resulting from reduced reserves of nitric oxide
(NO), the most important vasodilator substance that induces
relaxation of vascular smooth muscle (93). However, it is
not known whether these changes in SCH are solely due to
hypercholesterolemia-induced oxidative stress in the endo-
thelium, which in turn causes NO breakdown, or are the
result of synergistic inﬂuences of various CV risk factors.
Low NO levels (as well as TC, LDL-C, and hsCRP) were seen
to improve with LT4 therapy in one study (80). In any case,
the deﬁcient levels of NO are likely responsible for devel-
opment of hypertension and risk for atherosclerotic CVD in
SCH (93). A direct relationship of SCH to hypertension is
supported by data from Asvold et al . (94), demonstrating a
linear association between both systolic and diastolic blood
pressure and TSH levels within the ‘‘normal’’ reference range.
The thickness of the intima-medial layer of the carotid
arteries has been studied as a surrogate for atherosclerosis
and ischemic heart disease. Patients with SCH have been
found to have increased intima-medial thickness compared
to controls, and the degree of thickness was found to corre-
late directly to their LDL-C and TSH levels. LT4 therapy was
shown to reduce intima-medial thickness in parallel to ob-
served reductions in LDL-C and TSH levels (57).
SCH and CVD
The data on the risk of CVD in SCH are conﬂicting. Re-
cently, a meta-analysis based upon a systematic MEDLINE
search of studies conducted from 1966 to 2005 has indicated
that SCH is associated with an increased risk of CVD. The
risk was evident by sensitivity analysis of population-based
studies and in the subgroup analysis by type of study design
(95). Based on 4-year follow-up data, it has also been re-
ported in a study of 2730 men and women aged 70–79 years
that SCH (deﬁned as TSH levels above 7 mU =L) is associated
with an increased risk of congestive heart failure but not
with increased CV-related mortality (96). In another cross-
sectional study of 257 patients with a TSH >5m U=L, possi-
ble associations between SCH and atherosclerotic diseases
were investigated (97). Early results of the 6-year, but not the
10-year, follow-up study indicated that SCH was associated
with increased all-cause mortality in men but not in women.
The association of SCH with ischemic heart disease in men
was independent of age, systolic blood pressure, cholesterol,
diabetes, smoking, and BMI. This adverse effect of SCH on
outcome was not seen in another study investigating 3233
individuals aged 65 years or older with a TSH from 4.5 to
20 mU=L (98). Interpretation of the latter results is clouded
somewhat by the fact that a signiﬁcant percent of the patients
were started on thyroid hormone therapy during the follow-
up period, although the authors discount this concern by
statistical analysis. It is of interest that in a study of the oldest
old in Leiden, with 599 participants who were followed up
from age 85 years through age 89 years, increasing levels of
TSH were associated with lower mortality rate (99). These
ﬁndings suggest that oldest old patients with SCH may have a
more prolonged life span. Conceivably, survival beyond age
85 selects for healthier individuals with fewer comorbidities
that might otherwise compound the adverse effect of SCH.
Finally, in another study of patients with SCH, the restora-
tion of euthyroidism in the short-term does not decrease CV
risk (100).
Conclusion
The hypercholesterolemia and, more speciﬁcally, the ele-
vated TC =HDL-C and LDL-C =HDL-C ratios that are often
observed in SCH constitute risk factors for CVD that are
probably increased by the coexistence of hypertension, be-
ing overweight, or having insulin resistance, particularly in
middle-aged women. Compelling data show that plasma TC,
LDL-C, and apo B concentrations are elevated in SCH. The
increase in lipids is dependent upon the degree of thyroid
failure, and is more pronounced in patients with TSH levels
>10 mU=L or in those having elevated LDL-C at baseline.
Lower FT4 levels have been associated with increased CV
risk but this is not necessarily linked to raised TSH. Treat-
ment with LT4 leads to only a modest reduction of TC and
LDL-C, but should be considered for hypercholesterolemic
patients with SCH who are resistant to lifestyle modiﬁca-
tions. However, clear beneﬁt of a reduction in CV mortality
has yet to be demonstrated, and an adequately powered trial
of LT4 treatment on CV risk in SCH is needed.
Finally, in regard to other potential risk factors, the avail-
able data do not support any clinical utility in determination
of serum Hct levels in SCH patients with TSH <10 mU=L,
whereas CV risk appears to be ampliﬁed by insulin resistance
and the presence of other confounders. While studies of se-
rum hsCRP appear promising as a marker of CV inﬂamma-
tion in SCH, available evidence of an important role is lacking
and larger scale studies are needed.

第2页：双栏正文，介绍亚临床甲减的自然史与流行病学，综述其与总胆固醇、LDL胆固醇及脂蛋白变化的研究证据。

第4页：双栏治疗证据页，讨论确诊后左甲状腺素治疗的适应证及其对血脂的影响；纵向长表1汇总多项治疗研究的设计、疗程、TSH水平、血脂结果和证据等级。

第6页：双栏正文完成动脉功能和心血管事件证据的讨论，给出应按TSH水平及总体风险个体化处理的结论，并在页末开始参考文献。

第9页：三栏参考文献页，继续列出内皮功能、动脉僵硬、心血管事件和死亡风险研究。
